content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the problem of noisy label learning. The paper analyzes the training procedure and separates the training into two phases: 1) learning the noisy distribution and 2) overfitting to one-hot labels. Based on that, the paper then proposes two methods to estimate the noise transition matrix using a clean validation dataset. The paper also studies the problem where the NTM is not diagonal-maximum, and proposes a method to handle such cases that significantly improve the performance of existing approaches.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper provides novel insights into the training procedure of noisy label learning and separates the training into two phases. The paper then gives two ways to estimate the noise transition matrix based on the two phases.

2. The paper studies a setting where the noise transition matrix is not diagonal maximum. In such scenarios, previous methods could fail terribly, and the paper proposes a simple modification to address such an issue. Empirically, the modification significantly boosts the performance of previous approaches.

Weaknesses:
1. The proposed method relies on a separate clean validation dataset, which is not always available in practical settings.

2. The setting where NTM is non-diagonal-maximum also seems unrealistic to me. If the off-diagonal entry has a larger value, why not use that label as the clean label instead? Maybe there could be cases where we encounter conflicts among labels by re-assigning the correct label. But still, I don't see a very clear practical scenario that such a setting could happen.

3. The proposed method only works with previous noisy-label learning methods that rely on NTM. It is hard to extend the method to settings where the noises do not come from randomness.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The paper is written very clearly and the presentation is very clean. However, I feel that theorems are probably overused and most of the theoretical results could be stated in the main text.

Quality:
The two-phase observation and theoretical analysis are both very interesting. The improvement over existing methods on the non-diagonal-maximum setting is also quite significant. The comparison in the CDMM case is a little bit weak.

Novelty:
The two-phase observation is a novel contribution to the training procedure of noisy label learning.

Reproducibility:
The proposed method is easy to implement and the reproducibility seems solid.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the novelty of the approach and the observations made, even though the current method does not have strong empirical use cases, I still think its contribution is valuable.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This papers propose two methods to estimate the noise transition matrix in noisy label training. Both methods involve computing the confusion matrix of a trained model on a clean validation set. The first proposed methods leverages a model that has the best validation accuracy and the second method leverages a model that has fully memorized the training data.

The submission attempts to justify the proposed method by a few theorems. 

The writing quality is very low and grammar errors are all over the submission.

From my reading, the theoretical justification included in this paper is very much unsound and the empirical results are weak. I details the reason below and recommend a strong rejection.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Errors for the Theoretical Proof. 

The theorems are incorrect on two levels.
- The proposed method uses the confusion matrix on the validation set as an estimate for the noise transition matrix. The theorems say nothing about the model's behavior on the validation.
- Theorem 1 only says that the *expected value of the loss* will become the same as predicting the groudtruth noisy transition distribution and says nothing about the model's prediction for each individual sample. Based on this reason, there is no fundamental "phases" in the training process on a theoretical level, even though the authors find so in their empirical experiments.

Besides, assuming that the label noise is independent for each sample is a very strong assumption and probably corresponds to no realistic setting at all. Building theories on this assumption doesn't seem the most productive to me.

# Errors/Weakness of The empirical results
- the baseline methods do not use the validation data for selecting noisy examples. Comparing the proposed method with this baseline is unfair.
- Results on only done on MNIST and CIFAR10. I consider such scale of the empirical results to be very small in 2022 context.
- Bolding in Table 2 and 1 appears very disingenuous. When the baseline numbers are better, they are not bolded at all.

# Writing Critique
There are simply too many grammar errors. I list a few here.
- Abstract first sentence. "We model explicitly": unclear what explicitly even mean here.
- Intro third paragraph: "DNNs prior learn" -> "DNNs first learn"

The authors should also consider edit the current title, which reads very awkwardly.
content.summary_of_the_review: The submission is not well justified on either the theoretical or the empirical level and is written poorly. I recommend a strong reject.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors first show the noisy training process can be divided into two phrases, a learning phase and a memorization phase by using theoretical certifications and experiments. Then, the authors propose a method based on the noise transition matrix to address the problem that small-loss methods cannot work when NTM is not a column diagonally maximum matrix.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The idea of this paper is clear although the writing of this paper should be enhanced.
2. The authors notice the problem that small-loss methods do not work when “NTM is not a column diagonally-maximum matrix”. 

Weakness:
1. Two Theorem provide little new knowledges. For examples, “minimizing E[ℓ2] will force DNNs separately overfitting ... will converge to its one-hot noisy labels” has been well known in the research community, even fully random noisy labels [1].
2. For most of papers in learning with noisy labels, methods commonly assume no clean labels existed in the training dataset. Given clean labels, the problem “NTM is not a column diagonally-maximum matrix” is easily solved.  However, the difficulty is how to accurately estimate NTM without clean labels. 
3. Co-teaching only employs noisy labels, but the proposed method uses clean labels, so this comparison is unfair in section 5. 
4. In experiments, the proposed method only compares with some old baselines. Some new baselines like DivideMix [2], FINE [3], and VolMinNet [4] are missing. Experiments on real-world noisy datasets, e.g., Clothing1M are also missing.

[1] UNDERSTANDING DEEP LEARNING REQUIRES RE-THINKING GENERALIZATION, ICLR 2017
[2] DivideMix: Learning with Noisy Labels as Semi-supervised Learning. ICLR 2020
[3] FINE Samples for Learning with Noisy Labels. NeurIPS 2021
[4] Provably End-to-end Label-Noise Learning without Anchor Points. ICML 2021
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing of this paper should be improved, and many related works should be added. 

Quality is below the average. 

Novelty is not enough.

The proposed method is simple, and I suppose it can be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: Since the paper provides knowledge that has been well known in the community, and experiments are not sufficient for supporting claims, I do not recommend this paper.

content.title: Enhancing Robustness of Deep Networks Based on a Two-phase Model of Their Training with Noisy Labels
content.abstract: In this study we model explicitly the learning behavior of deep neural networks (DNNs) trained with noisy labels in image classification. Specifically, we show theoretically and experimentally that the training process can be divided into two phases: a learning phase in which the outputs of DNNs converge to a hidden noise distribution no matter whether the training samples are clean or noisy; and a memorization phase in which DNNs start to overfit until the output for each training sample converges to its corresponding noisy one-hot labels. This two-phase model enables us to develop two simple yet accurate methods that rely on the outputs of DNNs to estimate the noise transition matrix (NTM). It also enables us to resolve a pitfall of many existing methods for robust training under noisy labels based on the small-loss assumption, namely clean samples have smaller loss than noisy samples in the early training phase. We show that these methods fail when NTM is not a column diagonally-maximum matrix and that this pitfall can be fixed by modifying the small-loss assumption based on our NTM estimation methods.
